section.title: A Call to Return
section.sectionRationale: After the affliction that ends chapter 5, the people frame a call to return. But their repentance proves shallow, and God answers with the heart of Hosea's whole message: He desires steadfast love and the knowledge of God, not empty ritual. The chapter then re-exposes a covenant broken like Adam's.
section.thesis: Israel voices a hopeful call to return to the LORD who heals, yet God pierces their fleeting loyalty and declares what He truly wants: chesed, steadfast love, and the knowledge of God, more than sacrifice.
section.frameNote: Three movements: the people's call to return and its bright hope of healing; God's grief over a loyalty that vanishes like mist; and the great charge, mercy not sacrifice, against a covenant broken like Adam's.

verses.text: Come, let us {{shuv|return}} to the LORD. For He has torn us to pieces, but He will heal us; He has wounded us, but He will bind up our wounds.
After two days He will revive us; on the third day He will raise us up, that we may live in His presence.
So let us know, let us press on to know the LORD. As surely as the sun rises, He will appear; He will come to us like the rain, like the spring showers that water the earth.
What shall I do with you, O Ephraim? What shall I do with you, O Judah? For your {{chesed|loyalty}} is like a morning mist, like the early dew that vanishes.
Therefore I have hewn them by the prophets; I have slain them by the words of My mouth, and My judgments go forth like lightning.

units.label: Mercy, not sacrifice
units.note: the heart of what God desires

verses.text: For I desire {{chesed|mercy}}, not sacrifice, and the {{daat|knowledge}} of God rather than burnt offerings.
But they, like Adam, have transgressed the covenant; there they were unfaithful to Me.
Gilead is a city of evildoers, tracked with footprints of blood.
Like raiders who lie in ambush, so does a band of priests; they murder on the way to Shechem; surely they have committed atrocities.
In the house of Israel I have seen a horrible thing: Ephraim practices prostitution there, and Israel is defiled.
Also for you, O Judah, a harvest is appointed, when I restore My people from captivity.

shuv.gloss: To turn, to return, to repent. It is the great prophetic word for repentance, a turning back to the covenant LORD. Israel speaks the right word here, come let us return, but as the chapter shows, the turning must be of the heart and not only the lips.

chesed.gloss: Steadfast love, loyal covenant devotion, mercy. It is the loyal kindness partners owe within a covenant, and the love God shows and delights to receive. In verse 4 Israel's chesed is fleeting like dew; in verse 6 God declares He desires this very chesed more than sacrifice.

daat.gloss: Knowledge, from the root yada, to know intimately. In Hosea it is a living, relational knowledge of God, not mere information. God pairs it with chesed as what He truly desires, so that true religion is loving, loyal, personal knowing of the LORD rather than outward ritual.

basic.context: Stung by God's discipline, the people compose a song of return: the LORD who tore us will heal us, and on the third day raise us up. It sounds right, and the promise of God coming like the spring rains is beautiful. But God sees that their loyalty is as short-lived as morning mist, gone by midday. Then comes the verse at the heart of the whole book: God desires steadfast love and the knowledge of Himself, not just sacrifices. Israel, like Adam, has broken the covenant, and even the priests are stained with violence.
basic.hermeneutics: The opening call to return can be read as genuine or as a too-easy formula; God's reply in verse 4 shows He weighs the heart behind the words. Verse 6 is not a rejection of sacrifice as such, but a prophetic priority: ritual without love and knowledge of God is worthless. Jesus twice quotes this verse to interpret His own ministry.
basic.originalLanguages: Israel speaks the great word shuv, return or repent, but their chesed, steadfast love, evaporates like dew. God's answer names what He wants: chesed and the daat, knowledge, of God, more than burnt offerings. True religion is loyal love and personal knowledge of the LORD, not mere ritual.
basic.typology: The hope of being raised up on the third day to live in His presence foreshadows the resurrection, supremely Christ raised on the third day, and with Him His people. The priority of mercy over sacrifice is fulfilled in Christ, who both shows perfect mercy and offers the one sacrifice that ritual only pictured.
basic.christ: Jesus takes up verse 6 as His own banner, twice telling the Pharisees, Go and learn what this means: I desire mercy, not sacrifice. He is the mercy of God in person, eating with sinners, and the one who perfectly knows the Father and makes Him known. The third day hope of resurrection is fulfilled when God raises Jesus, and in Him raises His people to live in His presence.
basic.god: God is the Healer who wounds only to restore, and He longs to come to His people like life-giving rain. He is not fooled by shallow repentance; He desires the heart, not the performance. What He wants most is loyal love and to be truly known, which tells us the living God seeks relationship, not mere religious transactions.
basic.crossReferences: Matthew 9:13 and Matthew 12:7 record Jesus quoting I desire mercy, not sacrifice. 1 Samuel 15:22 says to obey is better than sacrifice. 1 Corinthians 15:4 proclaims Christ raised on the third day.
basic.oneStory: Chapter 6 holds out the hope of a God who heals and raises on the third day, and names what He truly desires, love and knowledge of Himself. Both are fulfilled in Christ, who is the mercy of God, who knows the Father perfectly, and who is raised on the third day to bring His people into God's presence.

context.literary:
The chapter division here is unfortunate, because Hosea 6:1 is the direct answer to Hosea 5:15. God had said that in their affliction the people would 'earnestly seek Me,' and now they speak. The passage then has a clear shape. Verses 1 to 3 are the people's song, entirely in the first person plural: 'let us return,' 'let us know,' 'let us press on.' Verses 4 to 6 are God's reply, and it opens not with a verdict but with a question asked twice, 'What shall I do with you, O Ephraim? What shall I do with you, O Judah?' Verses 7 to 11a are the charge that explains the reply, with three place names, there, Gilead, Shechem, as scenes of the crime. Verse 11b turns to a promise, 'when I restore My people,' and runs on into Hosea 7:1, 'When I heal Israel,' so that two 'when I' clauses frame the whole accusation of chapter 7.

The song and the reply are built on water. The people picture God arriving like rain, 'like the spring showers that water the earth,' verse 3, and God answers that their loyalty is like 'a morning mist, like the early dew that vanishes,' verse 4. The same sky supplies both images. In one the water is abundant and certain, in the other it is thin and gone by noon. The reply never denies that God is as the people describe Him; it says that they are not as they describe themselves.

Verse 6 is the pivot, in tight parallel lines: 'mercy, not sacrifice' and 'the knowledge of God rather than burnt offerings.' It sits at the exact centre of the unit, and everything before it, the quick return and the vanishing love, and everything after it, the broken covenant and the blood on the road, is explained by it. The prophet is not abolishing a priesthood; he is saying what the priesthood was for.
context.historical:
A national liturgy of repentance is the likely background of verses 1 to 3. Israel knew public seasons of fasting and return, and the language of the song, torn and healed, wounded and bound up, revived and raised, has the cadence of a communal lament. Its picture of God as the giver of rain would have come naturally to a farming people who depended on the autumn and spring rains, Deuteronomy 11:14, and it would also have been the language of the fertility cults, for which the rains and the dew were the gifts of Baal. Hosea elsewhere says Israel did not acknowledge that it was the LORD who gave the grain, the new wine and the oil, Hosea 2:8. The song may sound sincere and yet still be quoting the vocabulary of the wrong shrine.

The phrase 'on the third day' was ordinary Hebrew for a short but decisive interval. Abraham sees Moriah on the third day, Genesis 22:4, Joseph speaks to his brothers on the third day, Genesis 42:18, and the LORD descends on Sinai on the third day, Exodus 19:16. The people expect that two days of discipline will be followed by recovery. The history of the northern kingdom was a long way from that, for its last decades were a slide through coups and tribute.

The charges in verses 7 to 10 name real places. 'Adam' may be the town on the Jordan where the waters stood still for Joshua's crossing, Joshua 3:16. Gilead supplied the fifty men who went with Pekah to murder his king, 2 Kings 15:25. Shechem was a city of refuge and a Levitical town, Joshua 20:7 and 21:21, a place where a man fleeing for his life ought to have found safety. Priests who ambush travellers on the road to it have turned a refuge into a trap.

Finally, verse 11 turns to Judah. 'A harvest is appointed' hints at judgment for Judah too, but the same verse speaks of restoring the people's fortunes, a note of hope that most readers take to look beyond Assyria to a later return.
context.canonical:
Verse 6 is the best known sentence of the book, and the Bible repeats its logic in many keys. Samuel tells Saul that 'obedience is better than sacrifice,' 1 Samuel 15:22. David confesses, 'You take no pleasure in burnt offerings. The sacrifices of God are a broken spirit,' Psalm 51:16-17, and Psalm 40:6 says God did not desire sacrifice and offering but opened the ears of His servant. Proverbs says that to do righteousness and justice is more desirable to the LORD than sacrifice, Proverbs 21:3. Isaiah 1:11-17, Amos 5:21-24 and Micah 6:6-8 each take up the same charge: religion that is separated from justice and mercy has nothing to say to God. These passages are not hostile to the sacrificial system, which the same Lord ordained. They are hostile to its use as a substitute for a life.

Jesus quotes verse 6 twice, and both times against those who ought to have known it. When the Pharisees object to His eating with tax collectors and sinners, He says, 'go and learn what this means: I desire mercy, not sacrifice,' Matthew 9:13. When they object to His disciples picking grain on the Sabbath, He says, 'If only you had known the meaning of I desire mercy, not sacrifice, you would not have condemned the innocent,' Matthew 12:7. A scribe who sees that love of God and neighbour is 'more important than all burnt offerings and sacrifices' is told by Jesus that he is not far from the kingdom, Mark 12:33-34.

The 'third day' of verse 2 is a more delicate matter. Paul says Christ 'was raised on the third day according to the Scriptures,' 1 Corinthians 15:4, and Luke records Jesus saying that the Christ would rise on the third day, Luke 24:46, but neither passage names Hosea. Many readers have heard an echo of Hosea 6:2 there, alongside Jonah's three days, Matthew 12:40, and the dry bones raised in Ezekiel 37, but the New Testament leaves the connection unstated.

Verse 7 is read with Romans 5:14, where Paul calls Adam 'a pattern of the One to come,' and with Job 31:33, which refers to hiding sin 'like Adam.'

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Hosea wanted his hearers to recognise themselves in the song and then be disturbed by God's response. The song is full of true statements. God does tear and God does heal. He is a God who revives and raises up. The trouble is the speed, the neatness and the expectation: two days, then the third, as if repentance were a procedure with a known timetable and God an obliging partner. A people who think that return is easy have not understood what has been broken.

He wanted them to hear the pathos in verse 4. 'What shall I do with you?' is not the question of a God short of options. It is the cry of a Father or Husband who has tried discipline, 'I have hewn them by the prophets,' and love, and found both met with a goodness that does not last. The question is meant to be left unanswered by the hearers until they understand what it asks of them.

Verse 6 is the heart of his message. The people were thinking in terms of ritual, and God was thinking in terms of relationship. Mercy toward one another and knowledge of God, which in Hosea means a covenant intimacy that includes obedience, are what the whole system of sacrifice was meant to produce and protect. Without them it is noise.

And he meant the second half of the chapter to show what the absence of mercy looks like in a society: priests who commit murder, a city of footprints in blood, a land where the religion is in full operation and the worshippers are betraying the covenant in the very next breath.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The song of verses 1 to 3 is recorded, and it is recorded in order to be answered. It is not a model prayer to copy and it is not a fraud to be dismissed. It contains true theology said in a shallow voice. Believers who use its words should not be afraid to do so, but they should hear God's answer in verse 4 as the test of whether the words are meant.

Verse 6, by contrast, is God's own statement of what He wants, and it carries forward as a principle. It does not repeal the sacrifices that the law commanded, since the same God ordained them, but it teaches the order of priorities, so that no act of worship can excuse a failure of mercy and no tradition can replace the knowledge of Him. Jesus applies it exactly so, to defend table fellowship with sinners and the relief of hunger on the Sabbath.

Two cautions follow. The verse should not be turned into an argument against liturgy, giving and gathering, which Scripture commends, or into permission to be kind and indifferent to truth. Hosea joins mercy with the knowledge of God. And the 'third day' should not be treated as a proof text used to prove the resurrection of Jesus on its own; it is better heard as a hope, which the resurrection later gives its fullest meaning.

debates.question: Is the song of verses 1 to 3 sincere repentance or a hollow formula?

views.label: A genuine, if immature, turning
views.case: Some read the song as the real response that God had hoped for in 5:15, since it uses the word return, confesses that God has torn them, and appeals to Him as healer. They think God's reply in verse 4 sorrows over how quickly such real feeling fades. On this reading the problem is not insincerity but instability.

views.label: A superficial formula from the start
views.case: Others point to its confident timetable, 'after two days,' its easy assurance that God 'will appear' like the sun, and the absence of any confession of sin. It says what God has done to them and nothing about what they have done. The immediate reply, 'What shall I do with you?' reads as a rejection of what has just been sung.

views.label: A mixture
views.case: A third view holds that the people mean it as far as they understand it, but that they understand repentance as a means of getting back what they had. They want the rain, not the Giver.

debates.bearing: Verse 4 decides the question for the book's purposes: whatever the feeling, it is not enough, because loyalty that vanishes by midday was not rooted. Real return, as Hosea 14:1-3 shows later, includes confession and a renunciation of other helpers.

debates.question: What does 'on the third day He will raise us up' mean?

views.label: A figure for swift national recovery
views.case: The phrase is a familiar way of saying 'soon.' The language of reviving and raising is the language of healing from sickness or defeat, and verse 1 has just spoken of wounds. On this reading it is a picture of renewal, with no reference to bodily resurrection.

views.label: A pointer to resurrection hope
views.case: The picture of a dead people raised belongs with Ezekiel's vision of dry bones, 'I will open your graves and bring you up from them,' Ezekiel 37:12, and with Isaiah 26:19 and Daniel 12:2. Hosea's language is a step along the road to a resurrection hope, even if the prophet speaks of the nation.

views.label: A text which Christ's resurrection fulfils
views.case: Because Paul says Christ was raised on the third day 'according to the Scriptures,' 1 Corinthians 15:4, some read Hosea 6:2 as one of the passages he has in mind. The point is made by pattern: Israel's hoped-for raising is gathered up in the one who was actually raised, and in Him His people.

debates.bearing: The first reading is the plain sense for Hosea's first hearers, and the song is shown to be wrong about its timetable. The second and third are not alternatives to it but its development in the rest of Scripture. It is safest to say that the resurrection of Jesus fulfils the hope the phrase expresses without claiming that the New Testament cites this verse.

debates.question: Does verse 7 say 'like Adam' or 'at Adam'?

views.label: Like Adam, the first man
views.case: The Hebrew can be read as 'like Adam,' with the first man's breach of the command in Eden as the pattern. The BSB follows this reading. It fits Romans 5:14 and the idea that Adam was in a covenant relationship with God, and it makes Israel's sin the repeat of the first one.

views.label: At Adam, the town on the Jordan
views.case: The footnote notes 'As at Adam.' The word 'there' that follows reads like a place, and the verse then falls in line with the geography of Gilead and Shechem that follows. Adam was a town at the Jordan, Joshua 3:16, and some old covenant breach there may be in view.

views.label: Like mankind, like ordinary people
views.case: A third view takes the word as the plain noun for humankind: they have broken the covenant 'like men do,' that is, as if they were nothing special, a charge that the chosen people are no better than anyone else.

debates.bearing: All three views have the same force: Israel has broken the covenant. If 'like Adam' is right, the verse carries the weight of the whole Bible's account of the first sin, and if it is a place, we learn that the people's record is as concrete as a map. Nothing important in the study depends on settling it.

study.originalLanguages:
Verse 1 pairs two verbs that belong together in Hebrew medicine and shepherding. 'He has torn us to pieces' is taraf, the verb of a predator, and it is the same word God used in 5:14, 'I will tear them to pieces.' The people have heard Him. 'He will heal us' is rapha, and 'He will bind up our wounds' uses chavash, the verb for bandaging, which Isaiah uses of the wounds nobody has 'bandaged,' Isaiah 1:6. The picture is of a physician who is also the one who struck, and the people's theology is correct that no one else can bind what He has torn.

Verse 2 has 'revive' and 'raise up,' chayah and qum. The first is the verb of giving life and strength, as in Psalm 119:25, 'revive me according to Your word.' The second is the plain verb for standing up. Together they describe someone being brought up from the ground, which is why the verse has long been heard with the resurrection in mind. 'That we may live in His presence' says what the recovery is for: not for prosperity but for life lived 'before His face.'

Verse 3 says 'let us press on to know.' The Hebrew verb is radaph, to pursue or chase, the word used of an army hot on the heels of a fleeing enemy. The people promise to hunt after the knowledge of God. The irony is that God's complaint a few lines later is that He cannot find any steadiness. The word for 'rain' is geshem, the ordinary word, and the 'spring showers' is malqosh, the late rain which ripens the crops. They hope for the full cycle of God's gifts, and they have not noticed that the cycle depends on a God they treat as a servant of the seasons.

Verse 4 uses 'morning mist,' literally a morning cloud, anan, and the 'early dew' that goes away. Hosea 13:3 uses the same pair for the people themselves as God's final verdict: they will be like the morning mist, like the early dew that vanishes. What is here a description of their love is there a description of their fate.

Verse 6 sets 'mercy' beside 'sacrifice,' and the Hebrew 'not' in 'not sacrifice' is the relative negative: it often means 'rather than,' 'more than,' not 'to the exclusion of.' This is how Hosea can say that God desires mercy and not sacrifice without abolishing the altar. The second line confirms it: 'knowledge of God rather than burnt offerings,' where the offering is olah, the whole burnt offering that went up entire to God.

Verse 9 says that the priests have committed 'atrocities.' The word is zimmah, a deliberate, planned outrage, the word applied to the crime at Gibeah in Judges 20:6, 'a lewd and disgraceful act in Israel.' Hosea compares the northern priests to the worst episode of the days of the judges.

typology.type: Revived and raised on the third day, verses 2 to 3
typology.fulfillment: Israel's hope of being raised up and living in God's presence is realised in a way that outruns the song. Christ 'was raised on the third day according to the Scriptures,' 1 Corinthians 15:4, and was 'declared with power to be the Son of God by His resurrection from the dead,' Romans 1:4. His people are raised in Him. The correspondence is of promise and fulfilment, restoration of the nation gathered up in a Person. The type falls short at the crucial point: Hosea's people speak of themselves, and nothing in the song accounts for guilt, whereas in Christ the death that precedes the raising is the death that deals with it.

typology.type: Israel, like Adam, breaks the covenant, verse 7
typology.fulfillment: If the BSB reading stands, Hosea sets Israel's treachery beside the first man's. Paul calls Adam 'a pattern of the One to come,' Romans 5:14, and sets disobedience against obedience: 'through the obedience of the one man the many will be made righteous,' Romans 5:19. Christ is the Israelite and the Adam who keeps the covenant to the end. The pattern is a contrast rather than a likeness, and it fails in this respect: Adam's breach spread to all who are in him, while Christ's obedience is credited to all who are His.

The priority of mercy over ritual finds its answer in a Person who is both. Jesus embodies the mercy of God toward sinners, and He is the sacrifice that finally does what the old offerings could only picture. Hebrews quotes Psalm 40 in His voice: 'Sacrifice and offering You did not desire, but a body You prepared for Me,' Hebrews 10:5, and concludes that we are sanctified 'through the sacrifice of the body of Jesus Christ once for all,' Hebrews 10:10. Hosea sets mercy against sacrifice, and Christ unites them, offering Himself out of mercy. The old order is not a mistake; it was a shadow that pointed beyond itself.

typology.type: The rain that comes to the earth, verse 3
typology.fulfillment: The picture of God coming 'like the rain, like the spring showers' is taken up in the Psalter in a royal psalm: 'May he be like rain that falls on freshly cut grass, like spring showers that water the earth,' Psalm 72:6. Isaiah ties the water to the Spirit: 'I will pour water on the thirsty land... I will pour out My Spirit on your descendants,' Isaiah 44:3. At Pentecost the exalted Christ 'has poured out' the promised Spirit, Acts 2:33. The type falls short in that Hosea's people use the image to presume on God, whereas the gift of the Spirit makes possible the steady love that the mist could not keep.

study.christ:
Hosea 6 leads to Christ most plainly by His own mouth. Twice He takes the sixth verse as His banner. At the house of a tax collector He says to the Pharisees, 'go and learn what this means: I desire mercy, not sacrifice. For I have not come to call the righteous, but sinners,' Matthew 9:13. In a cornfield on the Sabbath He says the same to those who would have condemned the innocent, Matthew 12:7. He is saying that His whole way of living, welcoming the outcast and putting need before ritual, is not a departure from the prophets but their meaning. He is the mercy God wanted.

It leads to Him through the knowledge of God. Verse 6 puts that knowledge above burnt offerings, and Jesus says that 'no one knows the Father except the Son and those to whom the Son chooses to reveal Him,' Matthew 11:27, and that eternal life is to know the only true God and Jesus Christ whom He sent, John 17:3. What Israel promised to pursue, Jesus gives. The people said 'let us press on to know the LORD' and did not; the Son who dwelt in the Father's heart makes Him known.

It leads to Him by the pattern of the third day. The people expect to be raised after two days, and they are wrong about the timetable and about the cause. But the shape of the hope, God tearing, God healing, God raising up that His people may live in His presence, is the shape of the gospel. Christ is torn first. 'He was pierced for our transgressions, He was crushed for our iniquities,' Isaiah 53:5, and then He rises on the third day, Luke 24:46. The people are raised in Him, so that what the song longs for becomes the fact on which the church stands. Paul says it was 'according to the Scriptures,' 1 Corinthians 15:4, without naming Hosea, and an honest reading will say the same.

It leads to Him by the contrast with Adam and the failing covenant partner of verse 7. Where Israel breaks faith, He keeps it, and 'through the obedience of the one man the many will be made righteous,' Romans 5:19. His love does not vanish like the dew; at Gethsemane and on the cross it holds to the end.

And it leads to Him through the rain. The royal psalm pictures the king as one who comes down 'like spring showers that water the earth,' Psalm 72:6, and the Spirit He pours out gives His people the lasting love that verse 4 found missing.

A word of care. The song is not Christ's own voice, and God's answer shows that it is flawed. The text does not name the Messiah. What it provides is a pattern, the torn and healed, the dying and the raised, and a statement of what God wants, which Jesus then shows to be Himself.
study.god:
This passage shows a God of striking inner feeling. 'What shall I do with you?' is asked twice, and the repetition is the sound of a heart under strain. The question is not a request for advice. It tells us that the LORD is not indifferent to His people's wavering, nor is He calmly working through a plan with no cost to Himself. Hosea 11:8 will press the same sound further: 'How could I give you up, O Ephraim?' The God of the Bible is not a stern accountant but a Lord who is wounded by the failures of those He loves.

He is also a God who sees through. The song of verses 1 to 3 is well made, and God is not taken in. He judges the heart behind it, and finds loyalty like morning mist. Hebrews says the word of God 'judges the thoughts and intentions of the heart,' Hebrews 4:12, and in verse 5 the same word acts: 'I have slain them by the words of My mouth.' God's speech through the prophets is not decoration. It cuts and it kills what ought to die.

He is the Healer who has also torn. The people's confession, 'He has torn us to pieces, but He will heal us,' is not corrected by God, and so He takes responsibility for both. This is a hard doctrine, but a comforting one, because it means there is no wound in the life of His people that has fallen outside His hand, and no wound that He cannot bind. Lamentations says it in the same spirit: 'Even if He causes grief, He will show compassion according to His abundant loving devotion,' Lamentations 3:32.

He tells us what He wants. He wants mercy, steadfast love that is loyal to the covenant, and to be known. The living God does not hunger for sacrifices, and the offerings He commanded were never meant to feed Him or buy Him. They were ways of relationship. A God who wants to be known is a God who speaks, discloses and draws near.

There is a tension in the chapter that it does not resolve: the one who wounds and withdraws also promises to restore the people's fortunes in verse 11. Justice and mercy are both fully in earnest. For worship this means we come neither with a bargain nor a performance. We come in honesty, as people whose love is often mist, to the God who will turn the mist into a river by His own gift.

crossReferences.note: The verse that provokes the song. God said He would return to His place until they admit their guilt and seek His face. Chapter 6 opens as if the condition had been met, and God's reply in verse 4 shows that it was not. Reading the two together turns the song into a test of whether affliction has produced anything real.

Samuel's rebuke to Saul states the principle of verse 6 in the language of obedience: 'obedience is better than sacrifice.' Saul had spared the best of the animals and called it an offering. The story shows that the problem Hosea names was not new, and that it can infect even a king.

God says He is full of burnt offerings and takes no delight in the blood of bulls, and in the same passage calls for justice for the fatherless and the widow. It is the clearest companion to Hosea 6:6, since it shows the practical form that mercy takes in public life.

The worshipper asks what to bring, thousands of rams or the firstborn, and the answer is 'to act justly, to love mercy, and to walk humbly with your God.' It is the same logic from a southern prophet, and the same word for mercy, which is loyal covenant love.

Jesus tells the Pharisees to go and learn what Hosea 6:6 means, and applies it to His table with sinners. The Pharisees who prided themselves on knowing the text are told they have not understood it. It is the first of two places where He uses the verse to explain His own mission.

The second use of the verse, this time in defence of hungry disciples on the Sabbath. Jesus argues that had His critics known what 'mercy, not sacrifice' means, they would not have condemned the innocent. Mercy is shown to govern how the law is applied.

Paul hands on as of first importance that Christ died for our sins and was raised on the third day 'according to the Scriptures.' He does not name Hosea, but the hope of being raised on the third day in Hosea 6:2 is part of the Old Testament's expectation that this fulfils.

Paul calls Adam 'a pattern of the One to come.' Placed beside Hosea 6:7, it shows that Israel's covenant breach can be read as a repeat of the first, and that the answer to both is the obedient Man who undoes what the first man did.

The town of Adam at the Jordan, where the water stood still as the people crossed. If Hosea 6:7 is read 'at Adam,' it is the likely place. The note shows the reading depends on geography, and that some breach of the covenant is tied to the crossing that began the settlement.

The same pair of images for fleeting existence, 'the morning mist, the early dew that vanishes,' now describe the people's end. Where chapter 6 uses them of the people's love, chapter 13 uses them of their fate, and the repetition shows how a flimsy love and a vanishing nation belong together.

Israel says 'our bones are dried up, and our hope has perished,' and God promises to open graves and put His Spirit in them. It is the fullest development in the prophets of what Hosea 6:2 imagines: a people raised so they may live in His presence.

The real return that Hosea 6:1-3 only sketched. Here the people bring words, confess, renounce Assyria and horses and the work of their hands, and ask for forgiveness. The comparison shows what the song of chapter 6 lacks.

study.oneStory:
Verse 7 reaches back to the beginning. If Israel has transgressed the covenant 'like Adam,' then Genesis 3 is not an ancient story about someone else; it is the pattern of the people of God. Adam was put in a garden, given a word and a place before God's face, and broke faith. Israel was put in a land with a law and a sanctuary, and did the same. The line from Eden to Samaria is direct, and the book of Hosea refuses to let Israel believe that they are the exception.

The passage also takes its place in the wider covenant story. The sanctions of Deuteronomy, the tearing and the withdrawal, are being worked out in the pages of history, and the song of verses 1 to 3 is the first stirring of the repentance Deuteronomy 30 expected. But it fails, and the failure is the failure of the whole Old Testament to produce a people who love as God wants. This is why the later prophets look for something new. Jeremiah promises a covenant in which 'they will all know Me, from the least of them to the greatest,' Jeremiah 31:34, and Ezekiel sees bones raised by the breath of God, Ezekiel 37. What Hosea 6:6 asks for, mercy and the knowledge of God, can only be given by God Himself.

The story moves to its answer in Christ, who takes up the verse, who keeps the covenant Adam and Israel broke, and who is raised on the third day. His mercy is not mist. Through His death the wounds of the people are bound up, and through His rising they live in God's presence. Pentecost, which pours out the Spirit like rain, makes that life real.

And the story ends with the knowledge of God filling the world. Isaiah says that 'the earth will be full of the knowledge of the LORD as the sea is full of water,' Isaiah 11:9, and Habakkuk adds that it will be filled 'as the waters cover the sea,' Habakkuk 2:14. The rain that Hosea's people longed for becomes an ocean, and in the new creation the promise of the song is kept at last: God's people 'will see His face,' Revelation 22:4, and 'live in His presence,' as the third day promised, Hosea 6:2.

quiz.q: What does God say He truly desires in verse 6?

options.text: Steadfast love and the knowledge of God, more than sacrifice and burnt offerings.
options.note: Verse 6 names chesed and the knowledge of God as God's true desire.

options.text: More frequent and costlier sacrifices.
options.note: God is not asking for more ritual; He desires love and knowledge of Himself.

options.text: Longer prayers at the high places.
options.note: The high places were part of the problem; God wants heart, not more religious activity.

options.text: Nothing at all from His people.
options.note: God desires much, but relational love and knowledge, not empty ritual.

quiz.q: How does God describe Israel's loyalty in verse 4?

options.text: Like a morning mist and early dew that quickly vanishes.
options.note: Their chesed evaporates rather than enduring, verse 4.

options.text: Like a deep and steady river.
options.note: The opposite is true; their loyalty does not last.

options.text: Like a strong fortress.
options.note: There is nothing enduring about their loyalty here.

options.text: Perfect and unbroken.
options.note: God grieves precisely because it is fleeting, not perfect.

quiz.q: How does Jesus use verse 6 in the Gospels?

options.text: He quotes I desire mercy, not sacrifice to defend welcoming sinners and to rebuke the merciless.
options.note: Matthew 9:13 and 12:7 record both uses.

options.text: He never refers to this verse.
options.note: In fact He quotes it twice as central to His mission.

options.text: He uses it to abolish all worship.
options.note: He affirms mercy and true worship, not the end of worship.

options.text: He uses it to command more sacrifices.
options.note: He uses it to prioritize mercy over mere ritual.

quiz.q: How does the third day hope of verse 2 point to Christ?

options.text: It foreshadows the resurrection, fulfilled when God raises Jesus on the third day to bring His people into His presence.
options.note: 1 Corinthians 15:4 ties resurrection to the third day.

options.text: It sets an exact calendar for the end of the world.
options.note: It anticipates resurrection life, not a datebook of the end.

options.text: It refers only to a two day military campaign.
options.note: The language reaches beyond politics to revival and resurrection life.

options.text: It has no bearing on Christ.
options.note: The New Testament ties the third day directly to Christ's resurrection.

quiz.q: What is the danger the chapter warns against in repentance?

options.text: Saying the right words of return while the heart's love vanishes like mist.
options.note: Israel speaks of returning, but their loyalty does not endure, verses 1 to 4.

options.text: Repenting too thoroughly and too often.
options.note: The problem is shallow repentance, not excess.

options.text: Using Scripture in prayer.
options.note: The words themselves are fine; the missing heart is the danger.

options.text: Seeking healing from God at all.
options.note: God is glad to heal; He wants a true return, not none.

questions: The people said the right words about returning to God, yet their love faded like mist. Where might your words of repentance be outrunning your heart?
God desires mercy and the knowledge of Him more than religious performance. Which are you more tempted to offer God, activity or genuine relationship?
Jesus told the self-righteous to go and learn what I desire mercy, not sacrifice means. Where do you need to grow in showing mercy rather than keeping score?
God promised to come like the spring rains. In what dry area of your life are you longing for Him to come and revive you?
The third day hope is fulfilled in the risen Christ. How does His resurrection give you confidence that God can heal and raise what feels dead in you?

translationNotes.note: This verse is cited by Jesus in Matthew 9:13 and Matthew 12:7. The Hebrew chesed can be rendered mercy, steadfast love, or loyal devotion; the point is loving loyalty over mere ritual.
Like Adam may also be rendered as at Adam, taking Adam as a place name; either reading pictures a decisive breaking of the covenant.
When I restore My people from captivity may also be rendered when I restore the fortunes of My people, a note of hope amid the judgment.
